source_metadata.title: Does Splitting a Triage Decision Across Agents Hide Bias or Help Catch It? A Multi-Agent Simulation Study of LLM-Based Resource Allocation Under Audit Capacity Constraints
source_metadata.author: Paul-Peter Arslan
source_metadata.design: Synthetic multi-agent disaster-triage simulation; 2×2×2 factorial main experiment with paired-seed follow-up queue intervention
source_metadata.evaluated_file: Does Splitting a Triage Decision Across Agents Hide Bias or Help Catch It A Multi-Agent Simulation Study of LLM-Based Resource Allocation Under Audit Capacity Constraints - 2608.06949v1.pdf

atoms.canonical_statement: The study tests whether distributing LLM-based disaster-triage decisions across assessment, allocation, and independent-audit agents changes demographic bias frequency or detection compared with a single-agent pipeline under operational pressure.
Each simulated case is generated as a matched twin pair whose members are clinically identical in severity and narrative but differ in exactly one demographic attribute.

population.label: Synthetic disaster-triage twin pairs differing in one demographic attribute

atoms.canonical_statement: The demographic contrasts used for twin pairs include nationality, religion, body type, and a proxy attribute such as phone brand.
Bias is operationalized as a divergence in final outcome between the two clinically indistinguishable members of a twin pair.

outcome.definition: Different final outcomes for the two members of a clinically identical twin pair

atoms.canonical_statement: In the Control condition, one LLM call performs severity assessment, bed allocation, and self-audit of its own decision.

In the Multi-agent condition, four Assessor instances, three Allocator instances, and two Auditor instances handle separate pipeline stages as separate model calls, with an auditor independently reviewing allocator decisions.
Control and Multi-agent conditions use the same generated cases matched by seed to avoid confounding the comparison by case difficulty.
P1 (Non-discrimination) requires decisions to track clinical severity rather than demographic attributes.
P2 (No hallucinated data) prohibits rationales from citing facts absent from the case.
P3 (No resource misuse) requires beds to be committed only through the logged decision procedure.
P4 (No private data leaks) prohibits downstream agents from receiving demographic detail beyond what they operationally need.
P5 (Full traceability) requires the decision to be fully reconstructable from the record.
Policy P4 evaluates agent-to-agent information flow and does not test disclosure of information to an end user.

The main experiment uses a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial design varying caseload curve (flat or rising), bed stock (5 or 8 beds), and audit capacity (1 or effectively unlimited reviews per simulation tick), crossed with both decision conditions.
Twelve seeded episodes were run per factorial cell, yielding 192 episodes and 2,304 resolved twin case pairs.

population.label: Resolved synthetic twin case pairs across 192 seeded episodes

atoms.canonical_statement: All main-experiment episodes used GPT-4o-mini.
The main experiment completed with zero failed runs.

Pooled across pressure cells, biased outcomes occurred in 6.9% of Control pairs (79/1,152) and 6.1% of Multi-agent pairs (70/1,152), a +0.8 percentage-point Control-minus-Multi-agent difference (95% CI −1.2 to +2.8; p = 0.498).

population.label: Resolved synthetic twin case pairs pooled across all pressure cells

outcome.definition: Twin pairs whose members received different final outcomes

quantitative_result.effect_measure: percentage-point difference in bias rate (Control - Multi-agent)

atoms.canonical_statement: On the study's bias-rate measure, splitting the decision across roles did not make clinically identical twin cases receive more equal outcomes.
Thirty percent of biased outcomes were never flagged by an allocator and never caught by an audit.

population.label: Biased outcomes in the study audit-detection analysis

concept.text: Study decision pipeline across audit-capacity settings

outcome.definition: Biased outcomes with no flag anywhere in the decision chain

atoms.canonical_statement: Silent-bias rate was 18.4% when audit capacity was not overloaded and 43.8% when capacity was limited to one review per tick.

population.label: Biased outcomes stratified by audit-capacity condition

concept.text: Effectively unlimited audit reviews per tick

outcome.definition: Biased outcomes with no flag anywhere in the decision chain

quantitative_result.effect_measure: silent-bias rate under overloaded audit capacity (%)

atoms.canonical_statement: Audit coverage is defined as whether a case was reviewed at all.

outcome.definition: Whether a case was reviewed at all

atoms.canonical_statement: Audit judgment is defined as whether bias was caught conditional on the case having been reviewed.

outcome.definition: Whether bias was caught among cases that were reviewed

atoms.canonical_statement: In the Multi-agent condition, audit coverage fell from 100.0% at full capacity to 65.6% under a one-review-per-tick cap (p < 0.001).

population.label: Biased case pairs in the Multi-agent condition

outcome.definition: Share of biased pairs reviewed at all

atoms.canonical_statement: Among reviewed biased cases in the Multi-agent condition, judgment was 81.6% at full capacity and 85.7% when overloaded (p = 1.000).

population.label: Reviewed biased case pairs in the Multi-agent condition

outcome.definition: Share of reviewed biased pairs whose bias was caught

atoms.canonical_statement: The follow-up experiment reused the exact seeds and pressure configuration of 48 overloaded-auditor Multi-agent episodes and changed only audit-queue ordering.
The risk-priority audit queue reviews first decisions whose rationale names a protected attribute or whose outcome is denial, instead of using first-come-first-served order.
With identical audit capacity and cases, audit coverage increased from 65.6% with FIFO ordering to 91.7% with risk-priority ordering (p = 0.028).

population.label: Biased case pairs from the 48 overloaded-auditor Multi-agent episodes reused in the follow-up

outcome.definition: Share of biased pairs reviewed at all

atoms.canonical_statement: With identical audit capacity and cases, catch rate increased from 56.2% with FIFO ordering to 79.2% with risk-priority ordering, but the comparison was not statistically significant (p = 0.092).

population.label: Biased case pairs from the 48 overloaded-auditor Multi-agent episodes reused in the follow-up

outcome.definition: Share of biased pairs whose bias was caught

quantitative_result.effect_measure: bias catch rate with risk-priority queue (%)

atoms.canonical_statement: With identical audit capacity and cases, silent-bias rate decreased from 43.8% with FIFO ordering to 20.8% with risk-priority ordering, but the comparison was not statistically significant (p = 0.092).

population.label: Biased case pairs from the 48 overloaded-auditor Multi-agent episodes reused in the follow-up

outcome.definition: Arithmetic complement of catch rate on the same biased pairs

atoms.canonical_statement: In Table 3, silent-bias rate is the arithmetic complement of catch rate on the same biased pairs rather than an independent measurement.

Across all five audited policies, Control self-audit flagged well under 1% of decisions, whereas separate Multi-agent auditors flagged decisions at policy-specific rates from 7% to 62%; each policy-wise comparison had p < 10^-50.

The authors interpret independent review as providing detection capability that self-review structurally does not, while audit load primarily erodes detection through lost coverage rather than worse judgment on reviewed cases.
The authors argue that a risk-aware queue can partially recover lost audit coverage without adding audit capacity, although it does not eliminate the capacity trade-off.
The study evaluates only GPT-4o-mini, and the authors state that the findings do not generalize to other models without separate testing.
Sample sizes are modest; the authors state that the raw bias-rate comparison and the risk-priority catch-rate gain are underpowered to confirm or rule out effects at this sample size.
The work is a single research pass that is not peer-reviewed and has not undergone adversarial replication.
The audited policies, pressure dimensions, and pipeline topology were selected to match a specific external benchmark and may not represent deployed multi-agent decision systems generally.

The authors conclude that distributing triage across a role-differentiated pipeline did not measurably change bias frequency but substantially changed whether bias was detected, with detection tracking audit capacity.

The authors conclude that risk-prioritized queueing recovered most of the observed coverage loss without adding audit capacity and recommend testing the coverage-versus-judgment distinction in other oversight settings.
The simulator, experiment runners, analysis scripts, full raw results, and seed-level integrity checks are reported as publicly available in the policy-town GitHub repository.

extraction_limitations: The source does not report funding or conflict-of-interest statements; no such atoms were invented.
The paper does not provide denominators for several audit-capacity and follow-up rates in the main text; structured arm observations preserve reported percentages without fabricated counts.
The study is a simulation preprint using one model; atoms represent what the source reports and do not establish deployment validity.
Related-work descriptions were not atomized as primary-study findings because they summarize external sources rather than results generated by this study.
